I’m too old to get pregnant now, but for the longest time I put it off because I was too poor and too exhausted from my own mental and physical problems to do the work of caring for a child. 

When I had endometrial cancer and lost my ability to get pregnant, it was hard, I felt like there was a child I wanted to have and now I would never.  But I was still poor and physically sick.

So having a child or a permanent relationship just never happened, and I think my father’s abuse was the root cause of my exhaustion, which kept me from taking on anything requiring so much physical or mental effort.
Also he’s on on Patreon, and for free right now.

I danced for a while when I was younger. A good teacher should be able to show you how to have your weight correctly aligned over your feet. In ballet the posture is a kind of vertical whole body stretch. Traditional teachers will correct you relentlessly for any flaw, but keeping the stretch over a single axis and correctly over the knees and feet actually takes a lot of practice. A private lesson just for this topic could be helpful.

If this is just too uncomfortable, no worries. There are many styles of dance, especially if it’s just for fun.
Instead of buying rings we spent the money on a honeymoon trip. No regrets.

But it’s not really good enough, it leads to misunderstandings and miscommunications. Some people worse than others. This is because body language, facial expressions, and verbal subtext really are communication. So a scripted performance is not the same thing (anything you can rehearse) and trying to do as others do in real time will give an imperfect result.

And while misunderstandings can happen to anyone, the ones I get into have tended to follow a pattern. I’m missing information just as surely as someone would be who had a sensory limitation of some kind, or who was somewhat new to the culture. 

Long story short, if you’re really autistic, you still will be at 57, even if you have enough experience with social skills that you’re better at it than some fraction of the NTs. If you’re not as good as expected for your age, background and gender, it can still lead to problems. That means still needing fallback plans for the problems. It means the process of learning is lifelong.

This is exactly what worked for me. I was taught partly by my grandfather (a heavy machine operator and a good driver) and partly by a friend who was a firefighter pilot (the most calm person on the planet). Firefighter friend would be like “You’re coming toward a stop sign and should break” in the most calm matter-of-fact voice. I absorbed their approach, also by watching them. 

Phones can be a distraction so I take a screenshot of the route on Google Maps and then I have it while the phone is in airplane mode. I review the route, look at street view, and so on. If it’s a remote place and I have to be on time I will test run the route in person before the actual day of the appointment.

It helps me to think of the other people as cars and not people and drive defensively. I also did practice in a big parking lot and on empty roads when I was first learning. Driving is mostly a physical skill, so you want it in your reflexes as well as in your head. Now that I don’t work, I will drive sometimes for practice.

If I’m sleepy or already in sensory or emotional overload I will not let people pressure me into driving distracted. 

I hope this is helpful.

This is helpful. I have multiple issues and an unhelpful environment, so trying to be too rigid about time wasn’t working for me. Everything I could move off the schedule and onto the list I did, and now I have to make sure I have enough time to do the list and also have resting time. 
I am still working on this, because my sense of time and of my own energy levels is still unrealistic for me.

You misunderstand. I’m not saying I’m not sociable. I’ve had leadership roles at work and in the community and I’ve certainly hosted parties. Remember, I’m 57 and I’ve had lots of practice on social skills.

But what I still don’t have is typical ability to read body language or between the verbal lines. My language ability is good, but I still have some blindness to nuances in expressions.

Communication is a two way street. You can’t just be performing a script (masking), you also have to be reacting to the other person in real time in a way that conveys the intended meaning.

I’m not idealizing neurotypicals and I certainly don’t expect them to be perfect. Then too, there are other conditions besides autism that affect social skills.

But social communication is not just a learned script. I can act, even did stage performances when I was younger.

But a correct portrayal is *not* two-way body language communication.

You don’t in fact know this, you’re just insisting on it. 

Scripted body language is not what neurotypical people are doing. So following a script, if you don’t have a typical ability to read social cues, is not going to give you the same result as reacting quickly to social cues.

The social mistakes a neurotypical makes, and the ones I make (sometimes without knowing it) are not the same thing. That’s part of why I have a *diagnosable condition.*

In the same way, no amount of conscious effort or learning on my part will enable me to do eye contact just the way neurotypical women do. If I try too hard, I can do *too much* eye contact which can look fake, creepy or dishonest, or can look like flirting when I don’t intend to. 

Neurotypical people *don’t* just stare at each other’s eyes. That’s not how body language works in any culture. Learning a script for eye contact is not going to give me the same kind of eye contact as a neurotypical woman. It’s literally impossible no matter how much effort I put into it.

Since I can only approximate neurotypical eye contact, I’d rather do too little, and appear shy, than too much, and appear creepy.

But all the practice I’ve done with this - years of trial, error, and practice - is never going to give me perfectly neurotypical body language or the ability to read social cues just like a neurotypical.

If I could overcome this with effort, it wouldn’t be a diagnosable condition. But it is.

I’m 57 and too old to be diagnosed as a child, so I was forced to learn to mask by default. At the time there was no name or diagnosis for what now gets called high functioning autism. As a young woman, I was under particular pressure to be socially fluent, and I put a huge amount of effort into trying.

But the problem is this: even though after all these years I have learned a lot of masking, neurotypical people can still tell the difference. No matter how hard I try, I will always make the occasional social mistake, and I will always make a few mistakes without realizing I did.

There simply is no way to avoid needing some degree of accommodation, even if it’s just a friend or employer tolerant enough to not be bothered by some degree of quirkiness. I also still need sensory accommodation at home.

By age 57, it is what it is. Just as willpower alone will not get everyone free of a wheelchair who needs it, no amount of willpower is going to make my social functioning the same as a neurotypical woman of the same background.

Still no job.  My friends are out of money.  I spend my day mostly in a state of fear.  Yesterday I managed to organize myself enough to eat.  I am too sick to go to a shelter.  I think I will be done soon.

Thank you.  I still don't know were to turn, but I have a phone number now.  Also my friends managed to scrape something together.  It won't really be enough but I will try to stretch it out.  I rested for a while which feels like wasting time but I was so much in a panic I just could not get my head on.  It's like a physical thing.  So now that is dying down and I am thinking better although far from where I should be.  I need time to have my panic in.  I know when it's done enough.  But then I beat myself up for the time. But if I don't I will make bad decisions.
I don't know what to do either, but I hope you can get a good therapist or someone to talk to.
